hints: If the copy exists, it must start at some node of the big tree. Can you test one candidate starting node on its own?
Combine two DFS functions: same(a, b) checks two trees are identical, and an outer walk tries same(node, sub) at every node of root.

1. same(a, b): if either is null, return whether both are.
  2. Otherwise values must match and same must hold for both left children and both right children.
  3. Outer walk: if the node is null, return false.
  4. Return same(node, sub) or the walk on the left child or on the right child.

approaches.name: Brute force (used in the Java below)
approaches.idea: Try every node of root as a start and run the full same-tree check against sub.

approaches.name: Linear alternative
approaches.idea: Serialize both trees with markers for null children and search for sub's string inside root's string (KMP), or compare subtree hashes.

explain: In [5,3,8,1,4], starting at node 3 we compare it with [3,1,4]: values 3, 1 and 4 match and both 1 and 4 have no children, so the answer is true. In the second sample node 4 has a left child 2, so at node 3 the comparison of 4 with sub's leaf 4 fails because one side has a child and the other has null. The copy must include all descendants, which is why same checks null children too. The Java below uses the O(n·m) check, which is comfortably fast for 1000 nodes.
recognize: "Some node with all its descendants equals another tree" → for each node, run a same-tree DFS.
